activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Covering your ears with your hands makes loud sounds quieter.
story:
Emmett ran into the kitchen. He smelled something sweet. Mom was baking. "Blueberries!" he said. His nose knew.

Then Dad turned on the blender. It roared. It was so loud! Emmett jumped. "Too loud!" he said. He put his hands over his ears. The roar got smaller. The blender went on and on. Then Dad turned it off. Quiet! Emmett took his hands off his ears.

"How did it get quiet so fast?" he asked. "I covered my ears," he said. "My hands made the loud sound little!" He tried again. He clapped his hands over his ears. "Quiet, quiet, quiet," he whispered. He lifted them. He could hear Mom humming. Down came the hands. Quiet again!

"Can you help me?" asked Mom. Emmett looked at the blueberries. He touched one. It was cold and smooth. He tasted one. Sweet! "Yum," said Dad, tasting one too.

After his nap, Emmett heard the vacuum. It was loud and wild. He covered his ears with both hands. The vacuum sound got little. Then Mom began to sweep the floor. The broom went swish, swish. That sound was soft. Emmett took his hands down.

"I have two ears, two eyes, one nose, one tongue, and two hands," he counted. "That is me!"

"And me," said Dad, and he tickled Emmett's tummy. Emmett laughed out loud.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The counting words always go in the same order: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
story:
Riley wanted to help Grandma feed the hens. "You can toss the corn," said Grandma. "Count the hens so we know they all come."

Riley looked out at the yard. She counted, "One, two, four." Grandma laughed. "You jumped too far! After two comes three. Try again, slow."

Riley took a big breath. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten hens ran to her. Ten hens pecked the corn. "The words fit!" said Riley.

Then Riley saw something silly. A tiny hen hid under a warm blanket by the door. It was very quiet there. "One more makes eleven," said Grandma. Riley giggled. "Silly hen, you missed counting time."

The little hen fluffed her feathers to dry. Riley gave her a small handful of corn. The tiny hen pecked Riley's shoe. "That tickles!" said Riley. Grandma carried the hen back to the yard, and Riley waved. "Bye-bye, number eleven."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a clear, sunny day, the sky looks blue.
story:
Jasmine sat at her little table. She was drawing a picture. It was a picture of a party. A party in the grass, with cake and balloons.

Jasmine picked up a gray crayon. She wanted to draw the sky. Then she looked up at the window. The sun was shining big and bright. It was a sunny day. There was not one cloud. And the sky over the roofs was blue. Bright, bright blue.

Jasmine put the gray crayon down. She picked up the blue crayon instead. She drew the sky all blue, up and up and up. "Blue," she said. "Blue, blue, blue." She drew a yellow sun too. Then she drew red balloons. Then she drew green grass for the party.

Jasmine was hungry after all that drawing. Mommy called, "Snack time!" Jasmine marched to the kitchen with her picture. She held it up high. Mommy looked at the blue sky and smiled. "What a sunny day," said Mommy. Jasmine sat down and took a big bite of her apple. Outside the window, the sky stayed blue.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: At the playground, go down the slide feet first.
story:
Muffins were baking in the oven. Carter wanted to see them. He started to reach for the oven door. "Stop," said Mom. "It is hot." Mom held his hand. They stood back and watched together. The oven light glowed. Warm air moved out of the top. "Where is the cold spot?" Carter wondered. He found it by the door. It felt nice there.

Carter looked out the window. His big sister Lily was on the playground slide. She climbed up, up, up. Then she lay down on her tummy, head first. Carter tapped the glass. Lily sat up. She turned herself around. Her feet pointed down the slide. Whoosh! She went down feet first and landed on her feet.

"Did you see that?" said Carter. Mom smiled. The timer rang. The muffins were done. Mom used her big mitts to move the pan out. Carter smelled them from his safe, cold spot by the door. Then he and Mom sat down, and each ate one warm muffin.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Written music uses marks called notes to show which sounds to play.
story:
Felix went to the band room with his class. He saw a big drum and a small bell. He wanted to play the bell. "May I try?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Ana. "Take your time."

On the stand there was a paper. It had little dots and lines on it. "What are those dots?" Felix asked. Miss Ana smiled. "Those marks are called notes," she said. "Written music uses notes to show which sounds to play." Felix looked closely. He tapped the bell where the dots sat. Ding! He tapped again. Ding, ding! A bird sat by the window. It sang along. The notes climbed up the page, and Felix tapped higher sounds. Ding, ding, ding!

One dot looked tricky. Felix tapped the wrong spot. The sound was too low. He was a little upset. He took a breath. He waited. Then he found the right dot. Ding! The bird sang louder. "Again," said Felix. Ding, ding, ding!

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A referee watches the game and makes sure players follow the rules.
story:
Cooper put on his warm coat. Off to the ice rink! Mom and Dad came too. Grandma came too. Even his best friend Ruby came.

The players zoomed on the ice. Their helmets were blue and red. But one man had a striped shirt. He was not on a team. Cooper pointed. "Who is that?" he asked. Dad smiled. "That is the referee," he said. Cooper watched the referee. The referee watched the game. He watched and watched and watched.

Then a blue player pushed a red player. He pushed him right down! The referee blew his whistle. Toot! He held up his arm. The blue player had to sit down. Cooper jumped up and down. "The referee saw it! The referee saw it!" he shouted. Ruby clapped her hands.

After the game, they ate warm pretzels. Cooper held up his arm like the referee. Toot, he said, and laughed. "When I grow big, I will watch the game too. I will be the referee!" Grandma hugged him tight. "Best referee ever," she said.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: Some people close their eyes or bow their heads during a blessing.
story:
Jacob skipped into the kitchen. The table smelled like warm bread. Grandma was setting out bowls. Jacob clapped his hands.

"Soup night!" said Grandma. "First we say the blessing."

Jacob wanted to say it too. He wanted it so much. But he did not know how.

"Watch us," said Grandma. "Then you try."

Daddy stood by the table. Daddy closed his eyes. Daddy bowed his head. Grandpa did it too. His eyes closed. His head went down.

Jacob peeked. One eye open. He saw Grandpa's head bowed low. He saw Grandpa's eyes shut tight. Jacob closed his eye fast.

Grandma said the blessing. Her voice was soft like snow falling.

Now it was Jacob's turn. He squeezed his eyes shut. He bent his little head way down. "Thank you for the soup," he said. "Thank you for Grandma. Thank you for Grandpa. Thank you for Daddy. One, two, three, four!"

Nobody laughed at him. Everybody smiled.

"Jacob said it!" said Grandma.

"Jacob said the whole blessing," said Grandpa.

Jacob looked up. His eyes opened wide. "Again tomorrow?" he asked.

"Yes," said Daddy. "Every soup night."

Jacob sat up tall and picked up his spoon. "I love soup nights," he said.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: An ice cube feels cold when you touch it.
story:
Ruby went to the doctor with her mama. "The doctor will look at you," Mama said. "And I get a sticker after!" said Ruby.

First the doctor looked in Ruby's ears. "You hear with your ears," said the doctor. He rang a little bell. Ding, ding! Ruby heard it with her ears. Then he looked in Ruby's eyes. Ruby saw the light. It was bright! Then Ruby opened her mouth. "Say ahh," said the doctor. Ruby smelled the sticker sheet on his desk. It smelled like strawberries! The doctor touched Ruby's neck. His fingers were warm.

Then the doctor held out an ice cube. "You can touch it," he said. Ruby touched the ice cube. It felt cold! Ruby pulled her hand back fast. "Cold!" she laughed. She touched it again and giggled. Then the doctor said, "All done. What do we do now?" Ruby shouted, "Sticker time!" She picked a shiny red heart and stuck it on her hand.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Catching a big ball is easier with two hands than with one.
story:
Florence stood in the backyard with her red beanbag. She wanted to throw it into the hoop. Her big brother Sam held the hoop up low. Florence threw the beanbag. It fell on the grass. "Try again," said Sam. Florence picked it up. She threw it slowly this time. The beanbag went into the hoop. "Yay!" said Florence. She jumped up and down.

Then Sam brought out a big yellow ball. "Now catch," he said. He rolled it to her gently. Florence held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers. It rolled away under the tree. Florence ran after it. She tried one hand again. The ball fell again.

Sam sat down on the grass. "The wind can blow the ball," he said. "Want to try more?" Florence nodded. This time she held out both hands. She made a big round circle with her arms. Sam rolled the ball. Florence caught it! She did not drop it. "I got it!" she said.

Sam clapped. Their dog Rex woke up from being asleep by the fence. Rex ran over and barked at the ball. Florence laughed. She threw the ball high in the air. It landed right on Rex's head. Rex thought it was a new game. He pushed the ball back to Florence with his nose. Florence got ready with both hands.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your nose has two openings called nostrils.
story:
Jules was hungry. He wanted bread with honey. Mama got the bread from the top of the shelf. She cut it with the knife. Jules watched from his stool, far away.

The bread went in the toaster. Ping! It popped up. Jules heard the pop with his ears. "The toast is ready!" said Mama. Jules touched the plate. It was warm. His fingers could feel warm.

Jules sniffed the toast with his nose. "Mmm, it smells good," he said. "Where does the smell go in?" Mama smiled. "Your nose has two little openings. They are called nostrils." Jules touched his nose. He felt two soft holes, one and then two.

Jules ran to the mirror. He looked with his eyes. He counted. "One, two! I see my nostrils!" He sniffed again. Sniff, sniff. Could he smell with just one? He covered one nostril. The smell was small. He let go. The smell was big again!

He licked the honey toast with his tongue. Sweet! "Is it too late for more toast?" he asked. "No," said Mama, laughing. She dropped in two more slices. Jules knocked on the counter. Knock, knock, knock. Ping! The toast jumped up high, right past the top of the toaster.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: A recipe tells a cook what to use and what to do, one step at a time.
story:
Max put on his little blue apron. Today he would make pancakes for his family. Teacher Anna held up a big card with words. "This is a recipe," she said. "It tells us what to use and what to do, one step at a time."

Max looked at the recipe. Flour, eggs, milk. One cup, two cups, stir, stir. But Max was so excited that he skipped the eggs. He just stirred the flour and milk. His tummy rumbled. Pancakes, pancakes, soon!

Teacher Anna poured the batter onto the pan. Flip, flip. But Max's pancake came out flat. Flat as a rain puddle! Papa giggled. Mama giggled. "Oh no," said Max. "My pancake is sad."

"Let's read the recipe again," said Teacher Anna. They read it one step at a time. Flour, then eggs, then milk. Max cracked the eggs himself. Stir, stir, stir. This time the pancake puffed up big and round. "It's a happy pancake!" said Max. Papa took a big bite. "Mmm," he said. "One more, please!"

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: In the song 'Five Little Monkeys Jumping on the Bed', one monkey falls off each time, so the number gets one smaller.
story:
Edouard ran into the playroom. He clapped his hands. "Monkey time!" he shouted. He tipped out his toy box. Ten little monkeys fell out on the soft rug.

He lined up five monkeys on the bed. He counted them. "One, two, three, four, five!" Then he began to sing. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!"

He bumped one monkey onto the floor. The monkey sat in a bit of dirt by the rug. "Now four!" said Edouard. He sang again. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" He bumped one more off. "Now three!"

One monkey was alone on the floor. Edouard giggled. It was Mama's turn next. She came in and sang the last part with him. "No more monkeys jumping on the bed!"

Edouard hugged all the monkeys. "Let's do it again!"

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet.
story:
Kinsley wanted to paint a picture for Grandma. She got her paper and her blue paint. She sat close to Mama at the big table. Mama had a hot mug of cocoa. "Mine is hot," said Mama. "Yours is cold milk." Kinsley touched her own cup. It felt cool and nice.

Then Kinsley dropped her paint brush. It rolled away. It rolled behind the couch. Kinsley went to get it. She looked behind the couch. She saw a little box with holes in the wall. It was an outlet. Her fingers wiggled toward it.

Kinsley stopped. She did not touch it. She ran back to Mama. "There are holes in the wall," she said. "Behind the couch." Mama came right away. "That is an outlet," said Mama. "Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet. I will get your brush." Mama reached with a grown-up hand and got the brush out.

Kinsley sat down again. She painted big white flakes. "It looks like snow," said Mama. Kinsley smiled. "That is true," she said. "It snows at Grandma's house." She stayed right by Mama and painted until the whole page was full.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Up and down are opposites.
story:
Lucy ran into the playroom. "Look, Teddy!" she said. "A big slide!" The slide was tall. Beside it sat a small red slide for the dolls. Lucy put her friend Teddy at the top of the big slide. "You go first!" she said.

Lucy climbed up. She went up and up, one step, two steps, three steps. Then she sat at the top. "Wheee!" She slid down, fast. Teddy slid down too. "Fast!" laughed Lucy. Then she climbed up again. This time she went down very, very slow, like a sleepy snail. Mom brought warm cocoa. "Careful, it's hot," said Mom. Mom held the cup so nothing would spill. Lucy blew on it. "Now it's cold!" she said, opening her eyes wide.

"Up and down are opposites," said Mom. Lucy looked at the slide. She climbed up. She came down. Up, then down. She tried it again and again. "Teddy, watch me!" she called. She went up the ladder and slid down, fast, fast, fast.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Now means at this very moment.
story:
Arnaud ran to the story corner. He saw the big red robot book on the shelf. He wanted it now.

"Can we read the robot book now?" he asked.

Teacher Mia smiled. "Not now. Story time is after snack."

"But I want it now," said Arnaud.

"Now means at this very moment," said Teacher Mia. "Now we wash hands. Later we eat. Then the story comes."

Arnaud looked at the clock. He heard the water run. He filled his hands with soap bubbles. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop.

At the table, Arnaud ate his crackers. He heard a loud bell ring. That was the end of snack!

"Now?" he asked Teacher Mia.

"Now," she said.

Arnaud clapped. Yesterday the robot book was on the shelf all day. Today he waited, and then it happened. Tomorrow he would pick it first again.

Teacher Mia opened the book. The robot on the first page beeped hello.

"Hello, robot," said Arnaud.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Soon means in a little while.
story: Violet got to daycare. Her coat was cold from outside. She hung it on her hook. Teacher Mia said, "Snack time is soon." Violet sat down at the little table. She waited. Soon means in a little while, said her friend Ben. Violet tapped her feet. She looked out the window. A bird flew by. Then Teacher Mia rang the bell. Snack time came. It did not take long. Violet got a cup. Teacher Mia poured the milk for her. Violet ate her crackers. Yesterday, she had apples at snack. Today, she had crackers. Tomorrow, Teacher Mia said there would be bananas. After snack, the class went outside to paint. Violet painted a big red circle. "It has to dry," said Teacher Mia. "You can take it home later." Violet played in the sand while she waited. She poured sand from one cup to another. The wind blew a little. Then Teacher Mia called, "Paintings are dry now." Violet ran over. Her red circle was dry and shiny. She held it up. "Now I can take it home," she said. She carried it carefully to her hook, and put it in her cubby for later.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: You can start counting a group from any object, and the total stays the same.
story:
Sarah was at Grandma's house. Ten red apples sat in a big bowl. Sarah wanted to count them all by herself.

She started at the left side. One, two, three. She went slowly. Four, five, six. Grandma waited. Seven, eight, nine, ten. "Ten apples!" said Sarah.

Grandma poured milk into two cups. "Now let's count them again," she said. "Start at the other end this time."

Sarah started at the right side. One, two, three. She took her time. The cat watched from the chair. Four, five, six. Seven, eight, nine, ten.

Sarah put her hands on her cheeks. "Ten again! Ten both ways!" Grandma smiled and put one apple in each cup. "Ten again," said Sarah.

Then Grandma held up two plates. Cookies on one. Crackers on the other. "Which plate has more?"

Sarah counted the cookies. One, two, three, four, five. She counted the crackers. One, two, three. "The cookies!" she said. "The cookies have more!"

Grandma gave her a cookie. The dirty bowl went to the sink. Sarah ate her cookie and counted her bites. One, two, three. She laughed. "I can count anything!"

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Carry a pencil with the point facing down so it cannot poke anyone.
story:
Brielle got to school early. Teacher Mia put a pencil on her desk. "You can write your name," said Teacher Mia.

Brielle picked up the pencil. She held it tight and walked to the table. The point was up in the air. It waved near Leo's arm. "Careful," said Teacher Mia. "Carry a pencil with the point facing down."

Brielle turned the pencil around. The point went down, near the floor. She walked all the way to her chair. Nobody got poked. Then she held the pencil the way Teacher Mia showed her. She made a B. She made an R. Her letters were wiggly, but they were her letters. "Look, I wrote Brielle!" she said. Leo clapped for her.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Butter spread on warm toast melts.
story:
Paisley put on her little apron. The chef said, "You can wear it today." In the restaurant kitchen, the toast was ready. A grown-up had made it warm.

Paisley wanted to butter the toast all by herself. She took the knife. It was a safe, soft knife. She dipped it in the butter. She spread the butter on the warm toast. The butter went shiny. Then it melted away. Paisley looked and looked. "My butter is lost!" she said. The chef smiled. "Look again," he said. Paisley tipped the toast to the light. The butter was still there. It was shiny and wet and soft. Warm toast made the butter melt.

Next came the milk. Paisley held the cup with two hands. She poured slow, slow, slow. One drip ran down the side. But the cup did not spill over. "I did it!" said Paisley. The chef clapped his hands.

Outside the window, a tree moved in the wind. Paisley ate her warm, shiny toast. "More milk, please," she said.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: Clapping along to the beat means clapping at the same time as the beat of the music.
story:
Bennett ran into the music room. He wanted to clap and sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" all by himself. He tried it fast. He tried it slow. His claps went everywhere. The song went one way. His hands went another way. It did not sound right at all.

Miss Rosa sat down next to him. "Try this," she said. "Clap at the same time as the beat." Bennett put down his yellow cup of milk. He hid his hands under his legs and listened first. The song went clap, clap, clap. Then he let his hands out. He clapped when the song clapped. His hands and the music landed together, like two friends jumping at the same time.

"Now the song!" said Miss Rosa. Bennett sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." He did not stop clapping. Miss Rosa clapped too. Then everyone in the room clapped with them, all at the same time. Bennett sang louder. "How I wonder what you are!"

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Heavy and light are opposites.
story:
Josephine wanted to make a bed for the class bunny. She found a big box on the shelf. She pulled it. The box did not move. She pulled again. Still it stayed. "This box is heavy," said Ben. "It is too heavy for me."

Miss Dana came to help. "Heavy and light are opposites," she said. Together they pushed the big box down. It went slow, slow, slow. Then Josephine found a small pillow. It was light! She lifted it up high. She carried it fast across the room. She put it in the box so the bunny could sleep.

At snack time, Josephine drank cold milk. She touched the warm cup with her hands. The bunny snuggled into the pillow bed. Josephine gave the bunny a soft kiss on its head. "Sleep tight," she said.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Opposites are two words that mean things as different as they can be, like big and small.
story: Rehmat wanted to play the new game. Papa said, "I say a word. You shout its opposite. Opposites are two words that mean things as different as they can be." Rehmat nodded. Papa said, "Big." Rehmat looked around. She pointed at the big teddy bear. Then she held up her small duck. "Small!" she shouted. Papa laughed. Next Papa said, "Fast." Rehmat ran fast across the playroom. Then she walked slow, slow, slow. "Slow!" she said. Papa gave her warm milk. He held the hot cup himself. Rehmat touched her own cool cup. "Cold," she said, and took a sip. Then Papa said a tricky one. He said, "Happy." Rehmat thought hard. She made a grumpy face like her letter blocks had fallen down. Then she smiled big. "Grumpy's opposite is happy, so happy's opposite is grumpy!" Papa clapped. Rehmat gave him a hug. "Again," she said. "Say one more."

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: Tracing a letter's shape with your finger helps you learn how to write it.
story:
Audrey sat in the school library. She had a pencil and some paper. She wanted to write her name.

She wrote the A. She wrote the U. Then she came to the K. She drew it, but it looked wrong. The K was backwards. She tried again. It was still backwards. Her pencil was stuck in her hand, and she wanted to cry.

The teacher came over. She gave Audrey a card. The card had a big K on it. The K was bumpy. "Trace it with your finger," said the teacher. Audrey did. She moved her finger down the K. Then she moved her finger up and out, on both sides. She traced it again and again.

Then Audrey picked up her pencil. She wrote the K. It was right! She wrote her whole name: A-U-D-R-E-Y. Audrey held up her paper and smiled. "I did it!" she said, and she gave the teacher a big hug with both arms.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: Letters can be written as big capital letters or small lowercase letters.
story:
Evan ran to Grandma's house. On the wall hung big letters. A, B, C, all the way to Z. "I know that one!" said Evan. "A!"

Then Grandma opened a book. Evan looked at the page. He saw a little round shape. It looked new. It looked shy, hiding in the corner.

"That is not A," said Evan. "That is a different letter!"

Grandma smiled. "That is the same A," she said. "It is a small letter."

"Big A, small a," said Evan. "Same letter!"

"Yes!" said Grandma. "Letters can be big or small."

Evan jumped up and down. He said the letter sound. "Ah, ah, ah!" A feather drifted off the shelf. It made Evan giggle.

"Now the B!" said Evan. He began to climb onto the chair.

"Wait, I will hold you," said Grandma. She held his hand.

"B!" said Evan. "Big B, small b, same letter, buh, buh, buh!"

Grandma laughed. "My smart boy."

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: A book return slot is a place to drop off books when bringing them back to the library.
story:
Matthew held his mama's hand. The bookmobile was big and blue. It had wheels like a truck.

Inside, a lady smiled at Matthew. "Hello! Are you here for a library card?" Matthew nodded. He wanted a card so much. The lady typed on her computer. Then she gave him a little card with his name on it. Matthew picked a book about a red truck.

The next week, they went back. "Time to bring your book back," said Mama. Matthew hugged the book tight. "My book," he said. He did not want to let it go.

Mama pointed to a small door on the side of the bookmobile. "That is the return slot," she said. "We drop books there to bring them back." Matthew looked at the little door. He pushed his book in. The book slid down, out of sight.

Matthew felt his eyes get hot. Then he heard a soft thump inside. The lady opened the door from the inside. She held up his book! "Here it is, safe and sound," she said. Matthew laughed. The slot had taken the book to her!

He waved at the book. "Bye bye, truck book!" he sang. Then he picked a new one, about a big yellow bus. His smile was loose and happy all the way home.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: Singing a song while you scrub helps you keep washing long enough.
story:
Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. The dentist looked at her teeth. "All clean," he said. "Now you can pick a sticker and a snack."

Grace chose a red sticker. Then she saw apple slices on a tray. Her tummy made a hungry sound. "Wash your hands first," said the nurse. "Use soap. Wash for twenty seconds. That is a long wash."

Grace ran to the little sink. She made bubbles fast. She rinsed fast. "Done!" she said. The nurse shook her head. "That was too quick," she said. Grace frowned. Twenty seconds felt so long. How would she know?

Then Grace remembered camp. At camp they sang a song at the sink. The nurse smiled. "Sing it," she said. Grace sang while she scrubbed. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She scrubbed and sang. The song helped her keep going. When the song ended, she was done.

"Twenty seconds!" said the nurse. Grace looked at her hands. The bubbles had washed away. Where did the sticky jam hide? It was gone now. "My hands feel fuzzy clean," Grace said. She took an apple slice and crunched it. "Can we sing the song at home too?" she asked. "Every time," said Mom. Grace skipped to the door, still humming.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes.
story:
Sarah ran to the library play corner. There was a big red basket. There were tiny shirts in it. There were tiny socks in it. There was a tiny hat, too.

"Those are all clothes," said Miss Jo. "Clothes go in the basket."

Sarah grabbed the sock. She put it with the toy animals. She put it with the toy cars. Then she laughed and picked it up again. She dropped it in the basket with the shirt and the hat. All the clothes were together now.

Then Sarah found a book with a big picture of a puppy. The puppy had a rough, scratchy coat. Sarah could almost bend the soft page as she turned it.

"Again!" said Sarah. She pulled the clothes out one by one. Shirt. Sock. Hat. Then she sorted them all back in.

"Look, Miss Jo! Clothes!"

Miss Jo clapped. "Good sorting, Sarah."

Sarah hugged the book and grinned. "Puppy next!"

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Tracing over dotted letters is one way to practice making letter shapes.
story:
Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He had a big pencil in his hand. He wanted to write his name, all by himself. But the pencil wiggled and slipped. His M looked like a wiggly worm.

"I can't do it," said Max. His little brother was too young to write, but he watched from his high chair. Grandma put a paper in front of Max. The letters M, A and X were on it. But they were made of little dots. "Now trace the dots," said Grandma.

Max pressed the pencil down. He went dot to dot to dot. The dots made a big M. He traced again and again. Soon his hand felt steady. Then he tried a letter with no dots at all. It was an A. It came out just right.

"My turn," said Max. He wrote M, A, X on a clean paper. The pencil marks shined, wet and new. "Wait for them to dry," said Grandma. Max watched the shiny lines fade to soft gray. He held the paper up high. "Look, Grandma! That's my name!"

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: A blessing before a meal often says thank you for the food.
story:
Ivy went to the cemetery with Dad and Gran. They visited Gran Gran's stone. Gran laid down dry flowers. Then Gran unpacked a picnic on the grass.

"First we say our blessing," said Gran. Ivy folded her hands. Gran said, "Thank you for this food." Then they ate.

Ivy bit her apple. "Who grew my apple?" she asked. "A farmer far away," said Dad. Ivy thought hard. Somebody picked the apple. Somebody baked the bread. Somebody carried them all the way here.

Ivy wanted to say thank you too. But her mouth was full. She chewed and chewed. She swallowed. Too late! The blessing was done. Ivy felt a lump in her throat, like a stone.

"Can we say it again?" she asked. "Blessings can wait for you," said Gran. Ivy took a big breath. "Thank you for the apple. One, two, three, thank yous," she said. "For the farmer, the baker, and Gran Gran." Dad smiled wide. Gran wiped her eye with her sleeve. The wind moved the grass, soft and slow.

Then Ivy reached for the bread and took the biggest piece she could choose. "Gran Gran liked bread too," she said.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Rinsing your brush in water before a new colour keeps the colours clean.
story:
Zoe sat at the paint table. She wanted to make a green leaf for her tree painting. Green was her favourite colour of all.

She put yellow paint on her brush. Then she put blue on the same brush. She brushed it on the paper. But the green came out muddy and brown. "Oh no," said Zoe. "My leaf looks like mud."

Her friend Mia looked over. "Rinse your brush," Mia said. Zoe dipped her brush in the water cup. She swished it around. The water turned grey. She wiped the brush on a paper towel.

Now Zoe put yellow on the clean brush. Then she put blue. She brushed the paper. Bright green! Like a magic dragon, green and shiny. Zoe laughed and painted a big green leaf, then another, then ten more.

"Look," said Zoe politely to her teacher. "My tree has leaves." The teacher smiled. Zoe held up her brush. "Next, red and yellow," she said. "I will make dragon fire."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Covering your ears with your hands makes loud sounds quieter.
story:
Olivier sat in the doctor's waiting room. He was not late. Mommy had brought him on time. He looked at a picture of a plane on the wall with his eyes. He heard music playing with his ears.

Then the doctor's office door opened. Behind it, a big machine started to hum. It got very loud. Olivier did not like the loud sound. He covered his ears with his hands. The loud sound got quieter. He took his hands away. It was loud again. He put his hands back. Quiet again.

"Loud, quiet, loud, quiet," said Olivier.

"You found a trick," said Mommy with a smile.

Soon the big machine stopped. The waiting room was calm. The nurse called them in. "Open your mouth," said the doctor. Olivier stuck out his tongue. He touched a sticker with his finger. It felt bumpy. It smelled like strawberries.

The doctor gave him a paper to draw on. Olivier drew a plane and two big hands over two little ears.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Day and night are opposites.
story:
Lily was at school. It was nap time. The room was dark. "Is it night?" Lily whispered. She looked out the window. The sky was black. "It is dark like night," she said.

But then the teacher turned on a small light. The light was warm. Outside, the snow was cold on the glass. Lily touched the window with one finger. "Cold," she said. The light was not cold. The light was hot, so Teacher held it up high, away from little hands.

Lily wanted to know if it was night or morning. She got up slowly. She walked past the big blocks and the small blocks. One, two, three, four friends were sleeping. A snail sat in a jar. Its shell was big. Its body was slimy. "Hello, snail," said Lily.

The teacher smiled. "Look out now," she said. Lily looked. The sky was not black anymore. It was getting light. "Night goes away, and day comes," said the teacher. "Night and day are opposites." Lily watched the light grow. A bird flew by, fast. A cloud moved, slow. "It's morning!" Lily shouted. The snail slid up its jar. Lily clapped her hands. "One, two, three," she counted. "Three friends wake up!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Holding your nose closed makes food taste less strong.
story:
Milan was at the park with his dad. He saw a red berry basket on the picnic mat. "Can I taste one?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "They are sweet strawberries."

Milan picked one up. His eyes saw the bright red. His hands felt the bumpy little seeds. His nose smelled something sweet. His ears heard a bird singing in the tree.

Milan pinched his nose closed. Then he took a bite. He blinked. The strawberry tasted plain, like nothing much. He let go of his nose. Sniff! Now the sweet taste came back, strong again.

"Wow," he said. "My nose was closed and the taste went away!" He tried it again, just to know for sure. The taste got small again.

"How lucky I have a nose," said Milan. He took a big sniff of the basket. "My nose works like an elephant's big nose, right Dad?"

Dad laughed. "An elephant's nose can do even more. It can spray water!"

Milan held the last strawberry. He smelled it first. Then he ate it up.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: People wear hats, mittens, boots and warm coats to play in the snow.
story:
Abigail woke up and looked out the window. The world was white. "Snow!" she said. "No school today." Mom said, "We can go to the park." Abigail ran to get dressed. She put on her warm coat. She put on her boots. She put on her hat. She ran out the door.

At the park, Abigail made a big snowball. She clapped her mittens together. Then she stopped. "Where are my mittens?" Her hands were bare. Her fingers turned cold, then colder. They hurt. "Ow," said Abigail. "My fingers are too cold." Mom said, "Let's go back for your mittens." They walked home fast.

Abigail put on her mittens. Her fingers got warm again. Back at the park, she made snowballs with happy hands. Then she saw something in the snow. A small green frog sat there, with wide eyes. "Hello, frog," said Abigail. The frog hopped away, and Abigail waved. "Bye, frog!" she called.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: It is hard to see in the dark, so we turn on a light.
story:
Ivy had to wait for the doctor. She held her teddy on her lap. Then teddy fell down. He slipped under the big coat on the chair. The room was dark there. Ivy looked and looked. She could not see teddy.

"Let's be a team," said Nurse Ann. First Ivy used her eyes to look. Her ears heard the paper crinkle. Her nose smelled soap. She touched the soft coat with her hands. Still no teddy. "It is hard to see in the dark," said Nurse Ann. She reached up and turned on the light. The bright light made the dark corner bright. There was teddy!

"Now I can see him with my eyes," said Ivy. She hugged teddy tight. He was not grumpy at all. The doctor came in. He looked in Ivy's ears. He looked in her mouth. "Say ahh," he said. Ivy laughed. "Ahh," she said.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: Library books have a label on the spine that shows where the book belongs on the shelf.
story:
Luke put on his red shoes. Today he would get his very own library card! He ran into the storytime room. It had round rugs and big soft mats. Miss Kim smiled at him.

"Here is your card, Luke," she said. Luke held it with two hands. It was his! Now he could take a book home.

Luke found a book about a tiny seed that grows into a big sunflower. He loved it. But he put it back on the wrong shelf. Miss Kim turned the book. "See the label on the spine," she said. "It shows where the book belongs." The label had letters on it. Luke looked at the other books. They had labels too! He pushed his book next to the matching ones. It fit just right.

"Good job, Luke," said Miss Kim. Luke checked out his book. He hugged it all the way home. "Let's read it now!" he said.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Dogs, cows and fish are all animals.
story:
Isaiah went to the store with Mama. He wanted a stuffed animal. "Pick one!" said Mama.

First they walked past the toys. Balls and trucks sat on a long shelf. Then they saw the animal shelf. A dog! A cow! Isaiah hugged a soft dog. "This is an animal," he said. Mama smiled.

Next they passed the fish tank. A little fish swam round and round. "Fish is not an animal," said Isaiah. "It has no legs!" A big boy leaned close to the glass. "Fish are animals too," he said. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals." Isaiah's eyes got big. "Wow! The fish is an animal!"

Isaiah ran back to the shelf. He could not forget that fish. He picked the dog in one hand. Then he pointed at a fish toy. "Mama! Can I have an animal that swims?"

Mama laughed. "You can have both." She put the dog and the fish in the cart. Isaiah waved at the fish tank. "Bye, animal!" Then they went to get juice, and Isaiah held his fish all the way home.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Morning is the part of the day when we wake up and eat breakfast.
story:
Evelyn woke up. She heard the kettle. She saw Mom and Dad at the table. "Good morning," Evelyn said. Mom smiled wide. "It is morning now. That means we wake up and eat breakfast." Evelyn ate her egg. Then she said, "Now can we go to the park?"

"Today we can," said Mom. "Yesterday the park was wet from rain. Today it is dry." Evelyn put on her shoes. She took her present for Nia, a small red ball. She had gotten it yesterday.

At the park, Nia was already on the swing. "Good morning," Evelyn said. Nia laughed. "It is not morning now. We ate breakfast before, and now it is play time." Evelyn held out the red ball. "A present for you." Nia took it and hugged it.

They rolled the ball back and forth. Once it stopped in the grass. They waited. A wind came, and the grass moved, but the ball stayed. Evelyn ran and got it. They rolled it again and again. "Tomorrow we come back," said Nia. "Yes," said Evelyn. "Tomorrow." She threw the ball one more time, high and wide, and Nia caught it.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Other languages have their own words for thank you, like 'gracias' in Spanish.
story:
Elena woke up at Grandma's house. The kitchen smelled sweet. Grandma was baking cookies. Elena wanted one so much.

"May I have a cookie, please?" Elena asked. Grandma smiled and gave her a warm cookie. "Thank you," Elena said. The cookie was soft and yummy.

Then Grandma said, "Put on your shoes. We will go to the park before it gets late." The air was cool and fresh outside. At the park, a boy was digging in the sand. His shovel fell. Elena picked it up for him.

"Gracias," the boy said. Elena blinked. She did not know that word. "It means thank you," Grandma said softly. "Other languages have their own words for it." So thank you was not the same everywhere.

Elena tried the new word. "Gracias!" she said. The boy laughed and dug a big hole. Then he poured water in. "Look, it can swim," he said, floating his little boat on top. Elena clapped her hands.

On the walk home, Elena stepped on Grandma's toe by mistake. "Sorry," she said. "That's all right," said Grandma. At the door, Elena asked, "Can you help me with my coat, please?" Grandma helped her.

Then Grandma gave her one more cookie, right before dinner, just because. Elena held it in both hands. "Gracias," she said. Grandma hugged her tight.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: When you have a cold, resting in bed or on the couch helps your body get better.
story:
Arthur sat on the big couch. He had a sock on each foot and a warm blanket on his lap. His nose was red and his throat felt scratchy. He coughed one small cough.

"I want to run outside," said Arthur. He slid his feet to the floor. "Not yet," said Mama. "You have a cold. First we rest here. Then your body can get better." Arthur frowned. His face felt sour and grumpy.

Mama brought his favourite book. Arthur looked at the pictures. He found a cat, a moon, and a red boat. "Where is the frog?" he asked. He turned the page. There it was! Arthur let out a happy sound. He drank a little water from his cup.

He rested his head on the pillow. His eyes got heavy. He slept for a long time. When he woke up, he sniffed the air. Soup! His nose could smell again. He sat up tall. "My body feels better," said Arthur. He hugged the soft blanket tight. "Can we read the frog book one more time?"
